2.6 Fiscal Policy

Government revenue and spending

Section titled “Government revenue and spending”

Fiscal policy is the government’s choice of spending and taxes. Government spending includes the government purchases GGG of 2.1 Macroeconomic Data, but also transfer payments such as Social Security and Medicare, and interest on the debt.

The amount by which spending exceeds revenue is the budget deficit; each year’s deficit is financed by issuing government bonds, and the accumulated deficits are the government debt. The deficit excluding interest payments is the primary deficit: it reflects current spending and taxes, while interest is the result of past borrowing.

In fiscal year 2026 (October 2025 to September 2026), US federal revenue was about 5.40 trillion dollars and outlays about 7.40 trillion dollars, for a deficit of about 1.99 trillion dollars; net interest was about 1.14 trillion dollars (CBO, Monthly Budget Review, October 8, 2026). Federal debt held by the public is about 100% of GDP, the highest level since World War II (CBO, February 2026).

Fiscal multipliers

Section titled “Fiscal multipliers”

If the government spends one more dollar, by how much does output rise? The change in output divided by the change in spending or taxes is called the fiscal multiplier.

Lesson 2.4 Exercises Question 1 showed that, at a constant interest rate, when government purchases rise, producers’ income rises, they spend a share bbb of it (the marginal propensity to consume), which becomes someone else’s income, and so on. The government purchases multiplier is

kG=11−bk_G = \frac{1}{1 - b}kG​=1−b1​

Tax cuts also raise demand, but their effect differs from that of higher government purchases (Check C1).

Real-world multipliers are much smaller than this formula: part of income goes to taxes and part to imports, and interest rates may rise (next section). Empirical estimates vary widely, roughly between 0.5 and 2; multipliers are generally thought to be larger in a recession and at the zero lower bound, and smaller when the economy is near potential output.

Some fiscal policy needs no decision by the government: in a recession incomes fall, so income taxes fall and unemployment benefits rise automatically; in a boom the reverse happens. Taxes and spending that automatically move against economic fluctuations are each called an automatic stabilizer. They also make the multiplier smaller and so soften the effect of shocks (Exercises Question 2).

Check C1
With interest rates unchanged, cutting households' taxes by 100 has the same effect on output as raising government purchases by 100.
The 100 of government purchases is all direct demand. Do households spend all of a 100 tax cut?

Crowding out

Section titled “Crowding out”

When the government borrows to spend more, private investment may fall; this is called crowding out. There are two ways to see it, which are essentially the same:

  • Through interest rates: higher demand brings output close to or above its potential, the central bank raises rates to prevent inflation (2.5 Monetary Policy), and investment falls.
  • Through saving: a country’s saving is private saving plus government saving (a deficit is negative government saving). A larger deficit means less national saving, less money available for investment and a higher real interest rate.

How much crowding out there is depends on the state of the economy. Near potential output there is more crowding out, and a fiscal expansion mainly changes the composition of output (more government spending, less investment) rather than its total. In a recession at the zero lower bound, the central bank will not raise rates and much saving is idle, so there is less crowding out. In the long run, persistent deficits reduce capital accumulation and, by the Solow model of 2.2 Long-Run Growth, lower steady-state output per worker.

Check C2
The government raises its purchases, and the central bank, worried about overheating, raises interest rates. Compared with unchanged rates, the increase in output is:
Through which spending does the interest rate affect output in the IS curve? Which way does it move?
When rates rise, does firms' investment change? Does that change also work through the multiplier?
The central bank raises rates to curb overheating. Would it usually raise them enough to cancel the fiscal expansion, or more?

Debt sustainability

Section titled “Debt sustainability”

Let btb_tbt​ be government debt as a share of GDP at the end of year ttt, dtd_tdt​ the primary deficit as a share of GDP, rrr the average nominal interest rate on the debt and ggg the growth rate of nominal GDP. Debt grows with interest at rrr each year and GDP grows at ggg, so

bt+1=1+r1+g bt+dt+1b_{t+1} = \frac{1 + r}{1 + g}\,b_t + d_{t+1}bt+1​=1+g1+r​bt​+dt+1​

What drives the debt ratio is the gap between the interest rate and the growth rate, together with the primary deficit:

  • when r<gr < gr<g, the debt ratio can be stable even with a small primary deficit;
  • when r>gr > gr>g, the government must run a primary surplus, or the debt ratio rises without limit.

The primary deficit that keeps the debt ratio constant can be found from this equation (Check C3).

A debt ratio that rises without limit is not sustainable. In the end, either taxes are raised or spending is cut, or the government defaults, or inflation reduces the real value of the debt (inflation rate). The risk of the last two makes investors demand higher interest rates, and a higher rrr makes the debt even harder to sustain. For a country like the United States, which borrows in its own currency and whose bonds are treated worldwide as a safe asset, the risk of default is considered very low, but a rising interest burden squeezes other spending.

Ricardian equivalence

Section titled “Ricardian equivalence”

If the government cuts taxes today and borrows, it will have to raise taxes later to repay the debt. If households look far enough ahead, they will see that the tax cut does not raise their lifetime wealth: the extra money today exactly equals the present value of the extra taxes later (present value). So they save the whole tax cut to pay the future taxes, consumption does not change, and the tax cut has no effect on demand. This conclusion is called Ricardian equivalence: given government spending, financing it with taxes or with debt has the same effect.

Ricardian equivalence needs strong assumptions and usually does not fully hold in reality:

  • many households are liquidity-constrained and cannot borrow, so they spend a tax cut when they get it;
  • households may not look that far ahead, or may think future taxes will fall on others (the next generation, high earners);
  • taxes themselves change people’s behavior (the deadweight loss of 1.8 Welfare and Market Failure).

Empirical studies find that households spend part, but not all, of temporary tax cuts or payments; so tax cuts do stimulate, but usually less than government purchases of the same amount.

Check C4
Under Ricardian equivalence, when the government cuts taxes this year, issues bonds to cover it and raises taxes later to repay them, households save the tax cut and keep this year's consumption unchanged.
What are the future extra taxes worth today? Does the tax cut change households' lifetime wealth?

Summary

Section titled “Summary”
  • Deficit = spending − revenue; the primary deficit excludes interest. The US federal deficit in fiscal year 2026 was about 1.99 trillion dollars, net interest about 1.14 trillion dollars, and debt held by the public is about 100% of GDP.
  • In the simple model the government purchases multiplier is 11−b\frac{1}{1 - b}1−b1​; in reality taxes, imports, interest rates and the state of the economy usually make it much smaller. Automatic stabilizers soften fluctuations automatically.
  • Deficits can crowd out private investment, more so near potential output and less in recessions and at the zero lower bound.
  • Debt ratio: bt+1=1+r1+gbt+dt+1b_{t+1} = \frac{1 + r}{1 + g} b_t + d_{t+1}bt+1​=1+g1+r​bt​+dt+1​. When r>gr > gr>g, a primary surplus is needed to stabilize the debt ratio.
  • Ricardian equivalence: rational, far-sighted households save a tax cut; in reality it holds only in part.

Section titled “Exercises”
Question 1 ★
In the simple model Y=a+b(Y−T)+I+GY = a + b(Y - T) + I + GY=a+b(Y−T)+I+G (at a constant interest rate):
(a) Find the tax multiplier (its value when b=0.75b = 0.75b=0.75), and the change in output when the government raises both purchases and taxes by 100 (a balanced budget).
(b) Why can a balanced-budget expansion raise output?
Question 2
The marginal propensity to consume is b=0.8b = 0.8b=0.8. Compare two tax systems: (i) a fixed tax that does not depend on income; (ii) a tax of 25% of income, T=0.25YT = 0.25YT=0.25Y.
(a) What is the spending multiplier under each? If business investment suddenly falls by 100, by how much does output fall under each?
(b) Why is a proportional tax called an automatic stabilizer? What is its cost?
Question 3 ★
A government's debt is 100% of GDP, and the primary deficit is 3% of GDP each year.
(a) With an interest rate of 5% and nominal growth of 4%, what is the debt ratio after 10 years? What primary surplus is needed to keep the ratio at 100%?
(b) Suppose existing debt is all long-term fixed-rate bonds with an average rate of 4%; inflation rises unexpectedly by 2 percentage points, raising nominal growth from 4% to 6%, while the rate on existing debt stays the same for now. What primary deficit now keeps the ratio stable? Who bears the cost? Why can this not be done again and again?
Question 4
National saving = private saving + government saving (government saving = −deficit). The government cuts taxes by 200, raising the deficit by 200, with purchases unchanged.
(a) If Ricardian equivalence holds, by how much does national saving change? What if households save only 25% of the tax cut?
(b) A legislator says: "A tax cut leaves households more money, so it must stimulate the economy, and it does not affect business investment." Evaluate the statement in each of the two cases.
Question 5

(a) What percentage of outlays and of revenue is net interest? What is the primary deficit?
(b) Debt held by the public is about 31 trillion dollars, so each 1-point rise in the average rate on the debt eventually adds about 0.31 trillion dollars of interest a year. Why does a rising interest burden make fiscal policy less able to act in the next recession?
